content: The corrected stack is healthy with all three services. I’m now exercising the supported lifecycle rather than treating `compose up` as sufficient: local loopback health/version, public HTTPS/WSS upgrade, read-only and isolation invariants, `./ji status/down/up`, persistence across down/up, and non-interference with the existing Remote Host.

The remaining ingress failure is another least-privilege packaging conflict: the stock Caddy binary carries a low-port file capability, and Linux rejects executing it under `no-new-privileges` plus `cap_drop: ALL`, even though this deployment listens only on 8080. I’m verifying that capability and will remove it in a tiny JI-owned ingress image rather than granting an unnecessary capability.

The first loopback request raced the just-recreated ingress; the immediate retry succeeded, and all services remain up. I’m continuing with bounded readiness checks for the supported CLI lifecycle so that startup races are not hidden by fixed sleeps.

The public endpoints are returning the correct statuses; the prior shell checks misclassified successful responses because PowerShell treated `/dev/null` as a broken output target and array regex semantics mishandled the WSS headers. I’m re-running those assertions without changing the deployed system, then testing the supported down/up persistence cycle.

The supported CLI cycle retained the named metadata volume and restored all services healthy; the existing non-root `ji-host.service` stayed active. Next I’m binding the verification to the actual Remote Host/Relay interfaces and checking whether the Stage 4 Host has an already-supported Relay registration path—without changing the Host service or inventing a deployment-only bypass.

The installed Stage 4 Host correctly has no Relay environment, so I won’t mutate its unit or data. To verify the Remote Host topology without disturbing that accepted service, I’m checking the production connector’s observable presence/health contract and will run a separately named, temporary non-root Stage 5 Host against the deployed Relay if that contract can be verified without exposing access material.

The temporary topology uses the production `ji` distribution and the deployed public WSS endpoint, with separate data/ports and automatic cleanup. It leaves the accepted `ji-host.service` untouched; the one-use Host access token stays only in the temporary process environment and is never printed or redirected.

The first temporary-topology command was blocked before execution by the safety hook’s parsing of shell cleanup/`awk` syntax; no Remote Host probe started. I’m simplifying it to a unique JI-owned temp directory, Python cleanup, and `/proc` connection counts without positional shell expressions.

The remote shell has no system Java—which is an expected Stage 4 zero-prerequisite property—so the probe stopped before building or starting anything. I’m reusing the already verified bundled Java 21 runtime from the accepted Host installation, without altering that service.

The accepted bundle contains a JRE, not a compiler, so again no probe process started. I’m building the production `ji` distribution locally (where the full JDK is available), uploading only that non-secret distribution, and running it with the accepted remote Java 21 runtime.

The probe failed before starting the Host because the local ingress returned 502 while the Relay container was healthy—likely the ingress retained a stale upstream address across the prior Relay recreation/restart. I’m verifying that directly; if confirmed, the supported lifecycle must recreate or reload ingress when Relay is restarted, and the topology test should use the normal full-stack lifecycle rather than a service-only restart.
